key_insight: Membrane shape and tail/uropatagium geometry create clear aerodynamic trade-offs in gliding-mammal-inspired wings, affecting lift, stall behavior, drag, and control authority.
engineering_relevance: These results can guide the design of bioinspired morphing aerial robots by matching wing and tail morphology to the desired balance of efficiency, stability, and maneuverability.
method: Used computational fluid dynamics to isolate aerodynamic effects of representative gliding-mammal-inspired morphologies.
Compared three patagium configurations for lift, drag, stall, and pitching moment.
Tested three tail/uropatagium configurations under baseline, symmetric-deflection, and asymmetric-deflection conditions to assess longitudinal and lateral control authority.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparative CFD evaluation across multiple morphologies and deflection modes, with broader patagium giving the highest lift, intermediate shape giving smoother post-stall behavior, and different tail forms favoring pitch versus roll/yaw control.
watch_item: Results are based on controlled CFD conditions, so real-world performance may differ when structural flexibility, unsteady gusts, and full vehicle integration are included.
paper_title: Patagium and tail morphology shape aerodynamic performance and control authority in gliding-mammal-inspired wings
